text: Joab was told that the king was weeping and mourning over Absalom.
So the day's victory turned into mourning for the whole army, because word spread that the king was grieving for his son.
The troops slipped back into the city quietly that day, the way soldiers sneak back in shame after fleeing a battle.
The king covered his face and cried out loudly, my son Absalom, Absalom my son, my son!
Joab went in to the king and said he had humiliated all his officers who had that day rescued him and his sons, daughters, wives, and concubines.

Joab told him he loved those who hated him and hated those who loved him, and had shown that his commanders and men meant nothing to him — clearly he'd rather Absalom were alive and all the rest of them dead.

Joab warned him to get up and speak encouragingly to his men right now, swearing that if he didn't, not one soldier would stay with him by nightfall, a disaster worse than anything he'd already suffered.
So the king got up and took a seat at the city gate, and word went out that he was sitting there, and everyone came before him, while Israel's soldiers had already scattered to their homes.
All through Israel's tribes people were arguing that the king had rescued them from their enemies and the Philistines, and yet had fled the country because of Absalom.
And Absalom, the man they had crowned, was now dead in battle — so why was nobody talking about bringing the king back?
King David sent word to the priests Zadok and Abiathar to ask Judah's elders why they should be the last to bring the king home, when the rest of Israel was already talking about it.
He reminded them they were his own brothers, his own flesh and blood — why should they lag behind everyone else?
And tell Amasa, David said, that he is also his own flesh and blood, and that God would deal harshly with David if Amasa did not become his army commander in Joab's place from now on.
This won over the hearts of all Judah's men as if they were one person, and they sent for the king to come back with all his servants.
So the king started back and reached the Jordan, while Judah came down to Gilgal to meet him and help him cross.
Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand men from Benjamin came with him, along with Ziba, servant of Saul's household, and his fifteen sons and twenty servants, who rushed to the Jordan ahead of the king.
They crossed the ford to help bring the king's household over and do whatever he wished, and Shimei fell down before the king just as he was about to cross.
Shimei begged the king not to hold his wrongdoing against him or remember what he'd done the day the king left Jerusalem, asking him not to take it to heart.
He admitted he knew he had sinned, which was why he had come down that day, the very first of Joseph's whole house to meet the king.
Abishai son of Zeruiah spoke up, asking shouldn't Shimei be put to death for cursing the LORD's anointed king?

David answered that he wanted nothing to do with the sons of Zeruiah acting as his adversaries today — should anyone be executed in Israel on this day, when he knows he has just become king again over Israel?
Then the king told Shimei he would not die, and gave him his word under oath.
Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, also came down to meet the king; he had not washed his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he returned safely.
When he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, David asked him why he hadn't come along with him.
Mephibosheth answered that his own servant had deceived him — he had meant to saddle a donkey and ride along with the king, since he was lame, but his servant betrayed him.
His servant had slandered him to the king, he said, but the king was like an angel of God, so let him do whatever he thought was right.

He pointed out that all his father's family deserved nothing but death from the king, yet the king had given him a permanent seat at his own table — what right did he have to keep complaining to the king?
The king told him not to say anything more about it — he had decided that he and Ziba would split the land between them.
Mephibosheth said Ziba could have all of it, since all that mattered was that the king had come home safely.
Barzillai the Gileadite also came down from Rogelim and traveled with the king as far as the Jordan to see him across.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years, and had supplied the king with food during his stay at Mahanaim, since he was a wealthy man.
The king invited him to cross over and stay with him in Jerusalem, promising to provide for him there.
But Barzillai answered that he had few years left to live, so why go up to Jerusalem with the king?
At eighty, he said, he could barely tell good food from bad, or enjoy the voices of singers anymore — why should he be one more burden on the king?
He would just walk a little way past the Jordan with the king; there was no need for such a reward.
He asked to be allowed to go home and die in his own town near his parents' graves, but offered his son Chimham to go instead, for the king to treat however he saw fit.
The king agreed that Chimham would come with him, and promised to do for him whatever Barzillai wished, and anything else Barzillai wanted from him besides.
Then all the people crossed the Jordan, and so did the king; David kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and the old man went back home.
The king went on to Gilgal with Chimham beside him, escorted by all of Judah and about half of Israel's people.
Then all of Israel's men came to the king demanding to know why their brothers in Judah had stolen him away and brought him and his household across the Jordan without them.
Judah's men answered that the king was their close relative, so why get angry about it — had they eaten anything at the king's expense, or received any gift from him?

Israel's men replied that they had ten shares in the king, and more claim to David than Judah did — why had Judah looked down on them, when they were the first to suggest bringing the king back? But Judah's answers came back even harsher than Israel's.
